newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Italian lira battle foreshadows tough EMU talks.
newsitem.headline: Italian lira battle foreshadows tough EMU talks.

text.p: The battle to put the Italian lira back into Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism this weekend offered a glimpse of the hard political negotiations ahead for a common European currency.

What in the past may have been a technical matter, handled by well-seasoned and relatively anonymous EU bureacrats, the lira's re-entry into the ERM required a gathering of top policy-makers with an eye to the future.
As one senior monetary official put it: "One could imagine that the ERM is no longer what it was before Maastricht," he said of the Maastricht treaty that envisaged a single currency by 1999.
"In the present environment, everything is pertinent," he added.
Nothing, it seems, is more pertinent than ensuring that a common currency is launched with credibility and among countries with economic and budget policies that are sustainable.
But whether the negotiations over the lira offers any clue as to how the EU will look upon an EMU area that includes a large number of members is at this point unclear, says analysts.

"I haven't seen anything that would allow us to infer how they would treat southern Europe in relation to EMU," says economist Thomas Mayer at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt of the likely EU attitudes towards fellow southern European members Spain and Portugal.
Most say that while ERM membership is an important factor in assessing countries wanting to join a single currency, the real struggle will be on evaluating budgetary discipline.
The efforts being made to this end are considerable, not least in Italy, a country that has come a long way from the circumstances which caused its ignomonious ejection from the ERM in 1992.

Italy's EU partners appear to recognise this and the dangerous consequences of taking too tough a stance when it comes to currency matters. This awareness may stem from the lofty expectations in financial markets about EMU occuring on time and with a large group of members.
If one thing was clear during the 17 hours of talks this weekend it was that failure would have unleashed a severe market backlash, one that no one could probably afford.
While the debate over the rate against the mark was contentious, officials say it was influenced by a variety of factors, including confusion over a proper lira market value.

The clouded vision was compounded by the Bank of Italy's continued heavy intervention against the lira, a strategy designed to replenish its foreign exchange reserves. In recent weeks, the BOI's intervention had been enormous, serving to keep the lira just above the 1,000 level, sources said.
"The argument from the other side was that we accept this intervention, but it offers no clear view of where the market rate should be," said one official.
"But everybody agreed it should be below 1,000," he added.
Politically, the Italian side was under intense pressure to deliver a central rate above 1,000, and if it could not, there had to be seen as putting up the good fight.

The two factors forced an extraordinary meeting of EU finance ministers and central bank officials on Sunday, including Bundebank president Hans Tietmeyer, who was said to be an active participant in bilateral talks with the Italian side.
For its chances of joining a common currency in 1999, there was apparently a widespread, some say unanimous, view that ERM membership would have little influence.

Indeed both Tietmeyer and Dutch central bank chief Wim Duisenberg said as much after the meeting, stressing that acceptance into the ERM would not prejudge the decision in early 1998 on which countries participated in the single currency.
Perhaps the most suprising aspect of the marathon talks was France's relaxed attitude towards a central rate close to 1,000.
After rampant speculation that France would demand a parity rate of around 950, French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis told reporters they were happy to accept 1,000 against the mark.
Where did this change of heart come from?
One official speculated that a recent meeting between French President Jacques Chirac and Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi may have sealed such an agreement in advance.
